Clarity.justification: The paper follows a logical structure with clear hypothesis decomposition in tables and explicit separation of simulated vs. real results. Sections on mechanism validation and metric failure are articulated, but the heavy reliance on simulated data and abrupt transition to real-data failure create some confusion in following the narrative.

Novelty.justification: The core idea of linking contamination to representation invariance and confidence uniformity is a reasonable extension of existing behavioral detection methods, but the primary contribution is a negative result documenting the failure of the inverse-variance formulation. This is incremental rather than groundbreaking.

Soundness.justification: The majority of mechanism results (H-M1, H-M2, H-M3) are explicitly labeled SIMULATED and based on literature expectations rather than actual execution. The only real-data result (H-M4) shows complete failure (AUC=0.506). Code logs reveal runtime errors (device mismatch in representation.py) and incomplete training runs. The inverse-variance formulation is shown to amplify noise, with within-group std exceeding mean SSI at all levels.

Significance.justification: The paper addresses the important problem of paraphrase-resistant contamination detection, but the documented failure of the proposed metric and the simulation-reality gap primarily serve as a cautionary methodological lesson rather than advancing the field with a working solution or strong positive findings.

strengths: Clear articulation of the causal mechanism chain from contamination to confidence uniformity
Explicit identification of the simulation-reality gap as a methodological warning
weaknesses: Overwhelming reliance on simulated results instead of real experiments
Complete failure of the core SSI metric on actual inference data
Runtime errors and incomplete execution in provided code
